claims.statement: Octavia was Augustus’ sister and married Mark Antony. She tried to mediate between the two men as their alliance deteriorated. After Antony’s death, she brought up children from his marriages and his relationship with Cleopatra alongside her own family. Her household became part of the dynasty Augustus was building.

After Antony’s death, she brought up children from his marriages and his relationship with Cleopatra alongside her own family. Her household became part of the dynasty Augustus was building.

claims.statement: Octavia the Younger: 69 BCE to 11 BCE. Approximate lifespan. The plotted dates follow Livius’s 69 BCE birth and use 11 BCE from its alternative death dates of 11 or 10 BCE.

claims.statement: Livia married the future Augustus in 38 BCE and became an important adviser. Her son Tiberius eventually succeeded him. She continued to exercise influence after Augustus’ death. Hostile stories about her role in the family’s deaths should not be treated as established fact.

claims.statement: Ban Zhao was a scholar and teacher at the Eastern Han court. She helped complete the history of the Western Han after her brother Ban Gu died. Her writing also addressed women’s education and conduct. It gives us a named woman’s argument about family life, rather than a neutral account of how every household worked.

claims.statement: Plutarch describes Octavia arriving in Athens with money, clothing and soldiers for Antony. He told her to remain there. This records a particular journey in the breakdown of their marriage and political alliance. It does not provide a complete itinerary.

claims.statement: Octavia brings support to Athens: 35 BCE to 35 BCE. The Loeb edition’s footnote dates the arrival to 35 BCE. The map uses the Acropolis to locate Athens, not to claim that Octavia visited that monument.

claims.statement: Livia married Octavian, the future Augustus, in 38 BCE after her divorce from Tiberius Claudius Nero. Their marriage joined the family of her sons Tiberius and Drusus with the man who would become Rome’s first emperor.

claims.statement: Ban Zhao’s Lessons for Women discussed education, marriage and conduct. It combined an argument for women’s learning with expectations of obedience within the household. Read as advice, the text reveals the standards its author wanted women to follow. It cannot tell us how all women actually lived.
